nodes.label: The dispersal that succeeds
nodes.full: Somewhere around 60,000-50,000 BC, a separate Out-of-Africa dispersal succeeds where the Nubian Complex, Al Wusta and Alathar populations did not — its descendants are the ancestors of every non-African population alive today.
nodes.src: background; the broader Out-of-Africa genetics literature

nodes.label: Archaic hominins at Ti's al-Ghadah
nodes.full: Stone tools lie scattered among the butchered bones of elephants, jaguars and water birds at a fossil lakebed in the Nefud — the only dated Middle Pleistocene faunal assemblage known in Arabia. The interior was a wooded, lake-studded savanna, not desert, when they arrived.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Quaternary Science Reviews (2019)

nodes.label: An Nasim — the oldest dated Acheulean industry
nodes.full: Luminescence dating on lake and river sediments at An Nasim fixed a set of finely made handaxes to Marine Isotope Stage 9, a documented humid window — the first Arabian handaxe assemblage tied to an absolute date rather than typology alone.
nodes.src: Scerri, Groucutt et al., Scientific Reports (2021)

nodes.label: Homo sapiens crosses the Nefud — the Alathar footprints
nodes.full: Seven footprints pressed into the mud of a shrinking lakeshore, alongside elephant and camel tracks, are the earliest direct evidence of our own species in Arabia — a small group walking the lake margin, most likely to drink or forage.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Science Advances (2020)

nodes.label: The Nubian Complex reaches Dhofar
nodes.full: A distinctive Levallois core-reduction technique known from Sudan and the Horn of Africa turns up, largely unchanged, in the mountains of southern Oman — a lithic fingerprint for a population that crossed the southern Red Sea or Bab-el-Mandeb rather than the Sinai land bridge.
nodes.src: Rose et al., PLOS ONE (2011)

nodes.label: Al Wusta — a fossil finger bone
nodes.full: A single, directly dated intermediate phalanx — the only Arabian Homo sapiens fossil of this age — proves modern humans were living around the Nefud's lakes well before the genetically dominant migration out of Africa some 60,000-50,000 years ago.
nodes.src: Groucutt et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018)

nodes.label: Playas reform and people return to the Nefud
nodes.full: After millennia of Ice Age hyper-aridity had emptied northern Arabia, seasonal lakes reappeared and people followed the water back within a few centuries — leaving monumental engravings marking the routes between waterholes.
nodes.src: Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025)

nodes.label: Hominins and carnivores compete over the same kills
nodes.full: Stone-tool cut-marks and carnivore tooth-marks overlap on the same elephant bones at Ti's al-Ghadah — hominins and large predators were drawn to, and competed for, the same carcasses at the lake margin.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Quaternary Science Reviews (2019)

nodes.label: Dead-end dispersals and the disappearance of earlier populations
nodes.full: Neither the Nubian Complex population in Dhofar nor the Al Wusta and Alathar groups in the Nefud left detectable genetic descendants — each dispersal appears to have been absorbed, replaced or extinguished before the genetically successful migration of c.60,000-50,000 BC.
nodes.src: Groucutt et al. (2018); Rose et al. (2011)

nodes.label: Persistent places in an unstable landscape
nodes.full: Ti's al-Ghadah and An Nasim were revisited across tens of thousands of years and multiple humid phases — not single episodes but recurring anchor points fixed by a permanent water source, the closest thing this record offers to territorial memory.
nodes.src: Stewart et al. (2019); Scerri et al. (2021)

nodes.label: The band as the only visible social unit
nodes.full: Nothing in this record — no monumental architecture, no wealth differentiation in a grave, no specialised craft workshop — implies anything beyond small, mobile foraging bands.
nodes.src: argument from absence, stated explicitly

nodes.label: No confirmed art, ornament or deliberate burial
nodes.full: Unlike contemporary sites in Africa or Europe, no Arabian site of this age has yet produced confirmed symbolic material culture — this may reflect the state of research as much as an absence of the practice itself.
nodes.src: stated as an honest evidentiary gap

nodes.label: Monumental engravings at Jebel Arnaan, Mleiha and Misma
nodes.full: Across three newly surveyed outcrops, more than 60 panels carry 176 engravings — camels, ibex, gazelle, aurochs and wild equids, some over three metres long — cut into rock faces beside the resettlement-era lakes as markers of water and route.
nodes.src: Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025)

nodes.label: Speleothems record eight million years of climate
nodes.full: Uranium-series dating of 22 stalagmites from seven cave systems reconstructed a cycle of humid and arid phases stretching back 7.44 million years — the deep-time backbone against which every human dispersal into Arabia is now measured.
nodes.src: "Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past 8 million years", Nature (2025)

nodes.label: Reading a species from a footprint
nodes.full: With no bones to examine, the Alathar team identified the footprint-makers as Homo sapiens by comparing print size, shape and estimated stature and gait against a reference set of known human and Neanderthal tracks.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Science Advances (2020)

nodes.label: Luminescence dating opens the Pleistocene record
nodes.full: Optically stimulated luminescence — measuring the last time buried quartz grains saw sunlight — gave An Nasim's handaxes and the Nubian Complex tools of Dhofar their first absolute dates, moving Arabian prehistory into a chronometric science.
nodes.src: Rose et al. (2011); Scerri et al. (2021)

nodes.label: Megafauna hunting and scavenging at the lake edge
nodes.full: Butchered elephant, hippopotamus and water-bird bones at Ti's al-Ghadah show hominins working large and dangerous prey at the water's edge — the diet was built around the animals a permanent lake could support.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Quaternary Science Reviews (2019)

nodes.label: A foraging economy that follows the lake, not the season
nodes.full: Every dated site in this folio sits on a former lakeshore. Arabian foragers of this era were not desert specialists; they were lake-margin foragers whose entire range contracted or vanished with the water.
nodes.src: synthesis across Stewart, Groucutt and Scerri et al.

nodes.label: The Last Glacial Maximum empties northern Arabia
nodes.full: Hyper-aridity from roughly 25,000 BC mobilised the dune fields and drove out or killed off the human population of northern Arabia; no dated archaeological site anywhere in the region falls within this multi-millennium window.
nodes.src: Palaeodeserts Project regional survey; Guagnin et al. (2025)

nodes.label: The Nefud's playas reform and people return
nodes.full: Seasonal lakes re-established across the Nefud from around 14,000 BC — the first standing water there since the Last Glacial Maximum — and stratified camp sites show people moved back in within a few centuries of the water's return.
nodes.src: Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025)

nodes.label: Acheulean façonnage at An Nasim
nodes.full: The An Nasim handaxes are finely shaped by façonnage — flaking a whole cobble down to a symmetrical biface — showing Middle Pleistocene hominins here used locally distinct traditions, not a single uniform toolkit.
nodes.src: Scerri, Groucutt et al., Scientific Reports (2021)

nodes.label: Nubian Levallois point production
nodes.full: The Nubian Complex is a specific way of preparing a stone core to strike an elongated, triangular point in a single blow — otherwise known only from Sudan and the Horn of Africa, carried into Arabia essentially unchanged.
nodes.src: Rose et al., PLOS ONE (2011)

nodes.label: The southern route — Bab-el-Mandeb and the Nubian Complex
nodes.full: The Nubian Complex's presence in Dhofar, otherwise known only in North-East Africa, is the strongest single piece of evidence for a population crossing directly from the Horn of Africa into southern Arabia.
nodes.src: Rose et al., PLOS ONE (2011)

nodes.label: The northern route — Sinai, the Levant and the Nefud
nodes.full: The Alathar footprints and the Al Wusta finger bone sit on the other plausible corridor out of Africa — the Sinai land bridge into the Levant and down into northern Arabia — the route later used by the successful c.60,000 BC dispersal.
nodes.src: Groucutt et al. (2018); Stewart et al. (2020)

nodes.label: Arabia as the Africa-Eurasia crossroads
nodes.full: Arabia's recurring humid windows opened a corridor for mammal (and hominin) exchange between Africa and Eurasia — a biogeographic crossroads operating on a timescale far longer than any single human dispersal.
nodes.src: "Recurrent humid phases in Arabia", Nature (2025)

nodes.label: Dead ends: the dispersals that left no descendants
nodes.full: Genetic studies of living populations find no trace of the Nubian Complex, Al Wusta or Alathar groups — each appears to have been a successful but ultimately dead-end colonisation, absorbed or extinguished before the one dispersal whose descendants are alive today.
nodes.src: Groucutt et al. (2018); Stewart et al. (2020)

nodes.label: Eight million years of 'Green Arabia'
nodes.full: Long before any hominin arrived, Arabia was already cycling between desert and a 'green paradise' of permanent lakes, rivers, woodland and grassland — a pattern driven by slow shifts in Earth's orbit, repeating for millions of years.
nodes.src: Nature (2025), the speleothem study

nodes.label: A one-way trend toward aridity
nodes.full: Each humid cycle in the speleothem record is shorter and weaker than the one before it, tracking the wider global cooling of the last several million years — the modern Empty Quarter is where that trend has, for now, arrived.
nodes.src: Nature (2025)

nodes.label: A 42-metre lake in the Empty Quarter
nodes.full: A freshwater lake more than 1,100 km2 in area and 42 metres deep formed in the heart of what is now the Empty Quarter — fed by monsoon rains during the early Holocene humid phase, large enough that its overflow cut a 150km valley.
nodes.src: Afifi, Delaunay, Baby and Zaki (KAUST/Geneva, 2025)

nodes.label: The handoff to a settled Holocene
nodes.full: By the start of the Holocene the pattern that had governed Arabia for eight million years repeats one last time at human scale: the monsoon shifts north, the interior turns green, and — for the first time — people stay through it.
nodes.src: picked up by the Gulf-prehistory and Hejaz-prehistory folios

nodes.label: The footprint-makers of Alathar
nodes.full: Seven footprints — probably several adults and at least one child, moving together across drying mud — are as close as this record comes to watching specific, named-less people cross a landscape.
nodes.src: Stewart et al., Science Advances (2020)

nodes.label: One finger, one person, 85,000 years ago
nodes.full: The entire physical trace of this individual is a single bone from a finger — enough to identify the species, date the find and rewrite the migration timeline, but nothing about the person who once used that hand.
nodes.src: Groucutt et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018)

nodes.label: The invisible majority of a mobile world
nodes.full: Every named site in this folio is a rare accident of preservation at a former lakebed; the actual population — small mobile bands moving across a vast interior — left almost no trace at all.
nodes.src: Petraglia and colleagues, Palaeodeserts Project
